summary:
Bremen stands under the federal framework. The Self-Determination Act (Selbstbestimmungsgesetz, SBGG) passed the Bundestag by 374 votes to 251 and took effect on 1 November 2024, allowing adults over 18 to change their legal gender by self-determination rather than through the previous medical and court pathway; the change is entered in the civil registry, which in Bremen is processed by the city-state's own registry offices. Same-sex marriage has been legal in Germany since 1 October 2017. Bremen has no trans-specific statute or ordinance of its own, and federal criminal law and the General Act on Equal Treatment apply in the city-state without local deviation.

Custody is the sharpest documented exposure. Prison administration is a Land competence, and an analysis published on Verfassungsblog on 18 March 2026 found that all German Länder tie inmate placement to the prisoner's legal gender while § 6(1) SBGG permits state law to override the registry entry. Several Länder have enacted exception clauses, some written abstractly for all inmates and others criticised as targeted at trans prisoners; Bremen has enacted no placement statute of its own, so this national framework is the operative standard for any placement question arising in the city-state.

The exception has been applied in practice. A France24 wire report of 16 July 2026 covers the Liebich case, in which a prisoner was held in a men's prison despite a completed legal gender change. The case prompted Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia to launch a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal Self-Determination Act, placing the question on the legislative agenda for every Land, including Bremen.

Entry and screening do not turn on gender identity in Bremen, but a documented screening complaint exists elsewhere in Germany: DJ and producer BASHKKA filed a complaint under the General Act on Equal Treatment over a Frankfurt Airport screening of 23 November 2024 in which, as reported by Resident Advisor in June 2025, officers disregarded her gender identity in what she described as targeted transphobic harassment.
tangentialFactors:
The Liebich reporting has hardened the political climate around the Self-Determination Act. Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia responded to the case with a Bundesrat initiative to tighten the federal statute, and commentators cited in the coverage characterised the gender change as an abuse of the self-determination route. A visitor whose documents reflect a changed gender entry should expect that the entry may be contested by authorities rather than treated as settled.

Access to women-protected spaces has been contested nationally since the Self-Determination Act took effect. A Deutscher Sauna-Bund guideline of January 2025 restricting women's saunas to persons whose primary sex characteristics correspond set off sustained argument over registered trans women's access, and the same debate has run over leisure venues and, in Berlin, over an official information page from the prison service covering trans detainees. Federal law also bans conversion therapy for minors since May 2020, with penalties of up to one year's imprisonment and fines of €30,000 for offering, promoting or referring minors to such treatment.

Asylum and admission policy moved against LGBTI protection during 2025: in June the Federal Cabinet proposed designating Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia as safe countries of origin despite LGBTI people facing imprisonment there, and in August the governing coalition announced it would end humanitarian admission programmes including the Afghanistan scheme for persecuted LGBTI people.

Germany's public LGBT demonstration history runs through Bremen directly. The first Christopher Street Days were held in 1979, in Berlin with 400 partly masked participants and in Bremen, making Bremen one of the two original host cities of the format.
localsOnly:
Bremen's registry offices process gender-entry declarations under the unchanged federal Self-Determination Act; the city-state maintains no separate procedure, waiting period or documentation requirement of its own.

Because Bremen has enacted no prison-placement statute, inmates in the city-state's custodial system are placed under the general federal standard, with the § 6(1) SBGG override mechanism available to the Länder but not exercised by local legislation. Discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity is prohibited in health services and education under the General Act on Equal Treatment, in force since 18 August 2006, and the Federal Anti-Discrimination Office operates as the national complaint body.

The German STOP the HATE campaign maintains a counselling finder sorted by topic, emergency guidance including an LSBTIQ* crisis line, and a hate-crime knowledge base covering underreporting, evidence preservation, witness support and reporting channels.
outOfScopeNotes:
Unresolved: no Bremen-specific enforcement record for gender-based placement in custody, hate-crime reporting or discrimination complaints appears in the available sources; every operative standard cited here is federal or framework-level, and the sources do not indicate whether Bremen's prison administration has published guidance of the kind Berlin's prison service maintains for trans detainees.

Unresolved: the sources do not state how Bremen's registry offices handle declarations that conflict with a prison-placement decision, nor whether any Bremen court has ruled on the § 6(1) SBGG override. The France24 report establishes the placement outcome in the Liebich case but not the procedural route by which it was reached.

Not sourced: the inventory contains no data on violence against trans people in Bremen, no local figures on hate-crime incidence, and no information on the availability of gender-affirming care in the city-state. The historical material on Section 175 and the Nazi-era penalties is background to the federal criminal-law regime and does not describe any current Bremen practice.
